title: India's cooking oil imports reach a two year high in October as Diwali kitchens fill up
subtitle: Dealers estimate 1.74 million tons of palm, soybean and sunflower oil reached India in October, with soyoil at a record.
content_html:
Picture the big kadhai at your local sweet shop this Diwali, bubbling away as jalebis and namkeen fry. A lot of that oil sailed in on ships across the sea. In October 2026, India bought about 1.74 million tons of edible oil from other countries, 13% more than in September and the most in more than two years. The numbers are dealers' estimates, reported on 4 November 2026.

Edible oil simply means cooking oil: the palm, soybean and sunflower oil in the tins and pouches at your kirana shop. One ton is 1,000 kilos, so 1.74 million tons is about 1,740 million kilos of oil landing in a single month.

What came in by ship in October

Five dealers gave their estimates to the news agency Reuters, and the averages, published in Malaysia on 4 November, show all three big oils rising together:

  • Palm oil: 866,000 tons, up 6% on September and the highest since August 2025.
  • Soybean oil (soyoil): 653,000 tons, also up 6%, and the highest in any month on record.
  • Sunflower oil: 223,000 tons, double September's figure, which had been the lowest in more than four years.

Add the three and you get 1,742,000 tons, which is the 1.74 million total. A Ukrainian farm trade site, UkrAgroConsult, reports the same figures and calls the jump the highest monthly level in more than two years.

The dealers' number even beat an earlier forecast. A trade data firm, iGrain, had projected 1.66 million tons for October on 3 November.

Why so much, and why now?

The reports point to three reasons.

1. Festival cooking. Imports usually rise from September to November, when homes and commercial kitchens make more sweets, snacks and fried food. Diwali falls this month, and that is when the need for oil peaks, the ET report says.

2. Weather worries. Oilseeds are crops like soybean, groundnut and mustard that are crushed to make oil. This year, weather linked to El Nino, a natural weather pattern, damaged India's own oilseed crop. Rajesh Patel, managing partner at the trader GGN Research in Rajkot, told Reuters that worries about limited home supplies made demand even stronger.

3. Lower prices and a tax cut. Lower prices pushed refiners to buy more and build up stock before the festival. A refiner is a company that buys raw, unrefined oil and cleans it into the clear oil you buy in a bottle. A cut in import tax in September made the buying cheaper still.

The tax cut, in plain words

An import duty is a tax the government charges when goods enter the country. Think of it as an entry ticket that every tin of foreign oil has to buy at the port.

From 24 September 2026, the government lowered the basic customs duty on crude palm oil and crude soybean oil to 5% from 10%. On crude sunflower oil, the basic duty went to zero from 10%. Here "crude" just means raw cooking oil that still needs cleaning, not the crude oil that becomes petrol.

Two small extra charges ride on top (a farm infrastructure cess and a welfare surcharge). With them, the total duty on crude palm and soybean oil fell to 11% from 16.5%, and on crude sunflower oil to 5.5% from 16.5%. Refined palm and soybean oil now carry a basic duty of 27.5%, down from 32.5%, and refined sunflower oil 22.5%, down from 32.5%.

A simple way to see it: if a shipment of crude palm oil is valued at Rs 100, the tax on it used to be Rs 16.50. Now it is Rs 11. That Rs 5.50 saving on every Rs 100 adds up fast over thousands of tons.

Why is raw oil taxed far less than refined oil? The government said the changes were meant to cut import costs and ease prices for shoppers while keeping a tax edge for Indian refiners, according to the EconoTimes report.

From palm trees in Malaysia to your kadhai

India is the world's largest buyer of vegetable oil. Most of its palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia, while soyoil and sunflower oil come mainly from Argentina, Brazil, Russia and Ukraine, the ET report says.

India imports nearly two thirds of the vegetable oil it needs, Business Today reports. The bill is huge. The oil industry body known as the Solvent Extractors estimated the edible oil import bill would rise 9% to Rs 1.75 lakh crore in the marketing year ending October. A marketing year is the oil trade's own 12 month year, here running from November to October. The body linked the bigger bill to higher volumes and a weaker rupee.

A weaker rupee works like this. If a tin costs 10 dollars abroad and one dollar costs more rupees than before, the same tin costs more in rupees, even though its dollar price did not move.

Palm oil may keep flowing. Sandeep Bajoria, chief executive of the Mumbai brokerage Sunvin Group, told Reuters that palm imports are likely to stay high in November, because palm oil is cheaper than rival oils.

Will your cooking oil get cheaper?

The reports do not promise that. Vegetable oil prices in India have risen nearly 20% over the past year, the Angel One report notes. The lower tax cuts the landed cost, which is the full cost of the oil once it reaches an Indian port, counting its price, shipping and tax.

But the tax is only one part of the price. Business Today notes that retail prices will also depend on world oil prices, freight (the cost of shipping), the exchange rate of the rupee, home supply and the stock already in warehouses. It is like a samosa stall: even if the rent falls, the samosa may not get cheaper if potatoes and gas cost more.

Remember: these are early numbers

The October figures are dealers' estimates, not official data. The Solvent Extractors' body, which publishes India's official monthly oil import numbers, is due to release the October data by mid November. For September, that body reported imports of 1,544,447 tons, the EconoTimes report says. Going from about 1.54 million tons to 1.74 million tons is the 13% jump the dealers describe.

October shows how a tax change in Delhi, a festival at home and the weather on farms far away can each move the oil that ships carry into Indian ports, and the price of a plate of pakoras with it.
